title: NC State welcomes back Philip Rivers as new coach defends lack of time on college sideline
content:
Philip Rivers says the questions about his inexperience as he takes over as NC State’s head coach are fair. But he plans to “flood the building” with a staff full of coaches who have more experience in college football.

“The three most dangerous words are ‘I got it,’” Rivers said in his introductory news conference Monday. “I ain’t got it.”

He said he knows what he doesn’t know about coaching the college game but has the capacity to learn fast.

“I’ll be the first to acknowledge I have not sat in the seat of a head coach in college,” Rivers said. “I ain’t gonna sit very much.”

Rivers was introduced in front of a few hundred fans gathered in NC State’s indoor facility. At one point, “Sweet Home Alabama” played over the speakers. The stage was perched on the 17-yard line, a nod to Rivers’ jersey number, which was retired before he played his final game at NC State. Rivers arrived to the ceremony alongside his wife Tiffany, and spoke after opening remarks from NC State chancellor Kevin Howell and athletic director Boo Corrigan.

“He is one of us,” Howell said. “He knows what’s embedded in our DNA because he embodies it.”

Added Corrigan, “Philip Rivers is one of one.”

Rivers, when he took the mic, returned the phrase.

“NC State is one of one,” he said.

Many current NC State players attended the introduction, which lasted a little less than an hour. Rivers declined to detail his future plans for the roster or strategy in approaching the transfer portal, which opens on Jan. 4. He also declined to announce whether or not he would call plays, saying his philosophy and future staff would be announced as it came together.

Rivers announced his first hire Monday when he introduced former teammate Jatavis Sanders as his general manager. Sanders has been Alabama’s director of recruiting under general manager Courtney Morgan.

For the past six football seasons, Rivers has been the head coach at St. Michael Catholic High School in Fairhope, Ala. That run was interrupted by a three-game return to the NFL with the Indianapolis Colts in 2025, five years after he retired from pro football.

Rivers’ son, Gunner Rivers, was his starting quarterback at St. Michael. Gunner Rivers committed to NC State in February and is the nation’s No. 12 quarterback, according to 247Sports Composite Ranking. Philip Rivers said he and Corrigan discussed the question of how he could answer questions about his son with the university’s compliance department before Monday’s introduction.

“I cannot comment on the ’27 recruiting class, but our whole family is excited about coming to Raleigh,” Rivers said with a smile.

Rivers said the process of his family deciding to take the job was “emotional, thorough and healthy” and that he consulted his priest, mentors and extended family on leaving his home state to return to his alma mater.

Rivers started at quarterback at NC State from 2000 to ’03, closing his career as the ACC Player of the Year. He still holds the school records for career passing yards (13,484) and touchdowns (95).

“It’s hard to put into words what wearing that NC State red means,” Howell said. “But I know someone who understands it deeply.”

Rivers, who was overcome with emotion multiple times during his remarks, said his favorite part of playing was being a good teammate and that a foundation of his program would be coaching “the whole person” and finding coaches who believe the same. In his opening address, Rivers acknowledged his former head coach Chuck Amato, who died at 80 last month. His wife, Peggy, attended Monday’s event.

“I have to believe coach Chuck Amato is smiling down right now,” Rivers said. “I can hear him now, how fired up he would be.”

The Athletic reported earlier this fall that NC State’s 2026 roster cost between $22 million and $26 million; the midpoint of that range would rank sixth in the ACC. Rivers said resources were part of the discussion with Corrigan but not a sticking point.

“We don’t need to pull out spreadsheets and go through every penny,” he said. “It’s a belief we’re going to do everything we can to get NC State to the top.”

As for his inexperience, Rivers pointed to his time with Amato and in the NFL and said for much of his playing career, he felt he was an extension of a head coach. He acknowledged it doesn’t replicate the experience, but it does make the dynamic and the pressure more familiar.

“I feel like God has given me the gift to serve and impact through this game,” Rivers said. “And I’ve got a lot still to give. And there’s no place I’d rather give it than right here at NC State.”
